articles.text: Fourth of July Parade at 11 a.m. Saturday The long-awaited 59th annual 4th of July Parade will be held this Saturday, July 4, starting at 11:00 a.m. This year’s parade lands on the 250th anniversary of the United States of America, marking a significant milestone in the history of this nation. The Parade will set out from the intersection of Highland & Park Way with a procession of classic cars, marching bands, and a variety of floats by local clubs and organizations, and march to the far side of Piedmont Park. After the parade, Piedmont Park will host a community picnic and a musical performance by the Yacht Rockers. The Fourth of July Parade is Piedmont’s largest annual event, drawing an estimated 3000-4000 participants and viewers each year. The theme of this year’s parade is “Independence Day the Piedmont Way.” Parade entries prepare for friendly competition as they compete for the Highland Cup, Highland Saucer, Highland Spoons, and the ribbon awards. articles.text: As this year’s 4th of July Parade concludes, the community also marks the retirement of Kathy Kelleher as Chair of the 4th of July Parade Committee. For the past several years, Kathy has led the committee with dedication and enthusiasm, helping bring one of our community’s most cherished traditions to life. Except for 2020, when the parade was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Kathy has attended and planned more than 35 parades. Her connection to the event began in childhood, as her father, Dick Johnson, was the founder of the parade. Over the years, she has carried forward that legacy through her tireless commitment to preserving and growing this beloved community celebration. “We extend our heartfelt thanks to Kathy for her many years of service and for the countless hours she has devoted to making the 4th of July Parade a memorable event for generations of residents and visitors alike,” Kathy Kelleher said the members of the July 4th Parade Committee. As Kathy steps down, the committee has decided to appoint John Tulloch as the new chair of the 4th of July Parade Committee. Tulloch dedicated the majority of his career to serving local government and volunteering to help his city. He spent 17 years working for the City of Piedmont, stepping down in 2023 as Assistant City Administrator and City Clerk. He’s a newly appointed member of the Recreation Commission and is the incoming chair of the 4th of July Planning Committee.

articles.text: Starting on July 6, the block of Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland will be converted to one-way traffic heading northbound toward Oakland Avenue. The block will be closed to traffic on the morning of July 6, while the roadway is being restriped. Once the striping is complete the block will reopen as a one-way street. The conversion is the final of several measures the City has taken to improve safety, circulation, and the parking experience for visitors to the Civic Center. In addition to converting the street to one-way traffic, the new configuration will: • Eliminate the Havens Elementary drop-off zone on Bonita • Convert the parking spaces on the Havens Elementary side of the street from parallel to diagonal parking, which will add 17 new parking spaces • Add two new ADA parking spaces Earlier this year, the City added 30 additional time-limited parking spaces along Magnolia and Bonita Avenues. This doubled the short-term parking in the heart of the Civic Center. In an earlier phase, the City expanded the Havens Elementary School pick-up and drop-off areas on Highland Avenue, adding a second drop-off zone across the street from the school. The city’s goal is to improve safety and traffic flow in the Civic Center, particularly during school pick-up and drop-off hours, while providing the best possible experience for visitors. The City Council approved the circulation and parking changes in May 2025 after several months of discussion, including a community survey completed by 500 residents. The survey identified the expansion of short-term parking as a top need, with roughly half of respondents reporting parking in the Civic Center to be either “somewhat” or “very” difficult and over 80% of respondents reporting that they typically stay less than 2 hours. articles.text: Before starting a home improvement project that involves oil-based paint, stain, varnish, polyurethane, linseed oil, teak oil, or similar products, plan for safe storage and disposal of oily rags. As oil-based products dry, they release heat. When rags are bunched together, heat can build up and cause the rags to ignite without a spark or flame. This “spontaneous combustion” has caused multiple fires in Piedmont over the past three years. Piedmont Fire Department reminds residents, property owners, and contractors that oily rags should never be left in a pile, tossed in a trash can, or stored in a garage, shed, or work area without proper precautions. Always follow the instructions on the product you or your contractor uses. Before your next home improvement project, take a few minutes to plan for cleanup. If you are hiring someone to work on your property, talk to them about how they will store and dispose of oily rags during and after the job. Read and follow the disposal instructions on the paint, stain, varnish, oil, or solvent container. As oil-based products dry, they release heat. When rags are bunched together, the heat builds up and can ignite without a spark or flame. Plan where the oily rags will be safely stored while work is underway. Make sure oily rags are not left in piles, bags, trash cans, garages, sheds, or enclosed work areas. Confirm that oily rags will be removed from the property or handled safely at the end of each day. How to safely handle oily rags after using them: • Take rags outside and lay them flat in a single layer to dry. • Keep drying rags away from buildings, decks, fences, vehicles, and anything that can burn. • Weigh rags down so they do not blow away. • Once dry, place rags in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Follow the product manufacturer’s disposal instructions. Oily rags, oil-based paints, stains, solvents, and similar materials should not be placed in regular trash. Residents can use Alameda County household hazardous waste drop-off facilities for disposal of oil-based paints, stains, solvents, and similar materials. The closest drop-off facility is at 2100 East 7th Street in Oakland.
articles.title: Prevent house fires by making safe disposal of oily rags

articles.text: Zion Lutheran Church will host Tom Rigney and Flambeau for an afternoon arts and entertainment event on Saturday, August 29 at 5201 Park Blvd. in Piedmont. The concert is designed as a community-building cultural event, inviting neighbors, families, music lovers, and friends of Zion Lutheran Church to gather for an energetic live performance. articles.text: A family takes a quiet moment outside the Exploratorium, slowing down to observe, connect, and notice. One month into summer, and most parents have probably heard some version of it: “I’m bored.” Depending on the day, those two words can sound anywhere from mildly annoying to completely alarming. But what if boredom isn’t actually the problem? What if it’s part of the solution? My father was famously never bored. Wherever he went, he carried a sketchbook. Airports, waiting rooms, even meetings, he was always drawing; people sitting nearby, objects on a table, a view from a window. We still have books of those sketches. What I remember most isn’t that he was making art, it’s that he was paying attention. Many of his drawings were unfinished. Some were little more than scribbles. But sketching gave him a way to exercise curiosity, observation, and patience. He wasn’t waiting to be entertained. He was engaging with the world around him. In our household, that’s the version of boredom I’ve tried to pass along to my daughters. I’ve often told them that boredom is a choice—not because there is always something exciting happening, but because there is always something to notice. No matter where you are, there is something to wonder about, examine more closely, or learn from. The challenge isn’t finding something interesting, it’s learning how to direct your attention toward it. Summer gives us the opportunity to practice this skill. During the school year, much of children’s time is structured for them. Adults decide where they need to be, what they need to accomplish, and often what they should pay attention to. Summer creates pockets of unstructured time that can feel uncomfortable at first. Without a schedule to follow or an assignment to complete, young people are left with a different challenge: deciding for themselves what deserves their attention. Research shows that boredom can help kids build emotional resilience and independence. In one study tracking early childhood development, Alana Anderson and Sammy Perone found that learning to navigate the uncomfortable lull of boredom is a primary way children practice “effortful control,” the critical behavioral skill required to manage restlessness, brainstorm their own activities, and build internal motivation without relying on an adult or a screen to entertain them (Anderson & Perone, 2024). Additionally, when external stimulation drops, the brain shifts into what neuroscientists call the “default mode network,” a reflective state that encourages daydreaming, connection-making, and problem-solving, making an empty afternoon the ultimate workspace for independent imagination. This summer, let your kids get bored, but also encourage them to get themselves un-bored. Resist the urge to stimulate or entertain your child when they tell you they’re bored. Instead, ask what they’ve noticed today that they hadn’t noticed before. Ask what they’re curious about. Ask what they’ve always wondered but never taken the time to investigate. At the Exploratorium, we often talk about curiosity as a habit. Like any habit, it grows stronger with practice. So this summer, don’t rush to fill every empty moment. Leave a little room for wondering and noticing. Sometimes the most important summer learning starts when there’s nothing planned at all. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery: that real learning lives not in what we’re told, but in what we touch, question, and experience for ourselves—in classrooms, communities, and the curious moments of daily life.
articles.title: In defense of boredom

articles.text: There will a new administrative team at Piedmont Middle School (PMS) next year as Jamie Van Kleeck takes over as Principal. In his 12th year with the district Adam Saville moves from Tech Specialist to the role of Vice “We are in the midst of a generational shift of sorts at the middle school with many veteran PMS teachers retiring and many new teachers joining us,” said Saville and Van Kleeck said they will approach the opportunity with great enthusiasm and great humility. Change will come tangibly with electives for middle school students. A one semester Health class is being moved from 7th to 8th grade. During the April 15 school board meeting Van Kleeck explained that the health teacher agreed 8th grade is a “developmentally more appropriate time” for the Health content. Next year the middle school will pilot four new one semester elective courses: • Debate • Forensics • LEAD (Leadership, Empowerment, Action, Development) • Life Lab Next year’s Principal at PMS Jamie Van Kleeck (second from left) went on the Spring Break Trip to China with staff members PMS Core 6 teacher Lea Lotia (left), and PMS/PHS Mandarin teacher Xinjia Xia (right). Supt. Jennifer Hawn and high school principal David Yoshihara also went on a hike through the rice terraces of Guangxi. New PMS Vice Principal Adam Saville LEAD will focus on personal leadership, collaboration on meaningful initiatives, and reflection on growth as leaders. Life Lab will focus on practical skills such as cooking, financial literacy, basic home maintenance and gardening. Next year the middle school will also introduce a “zero” period (before school) PE for 7th/8th graders. This creative solution allows middle school students the option to take P.E. during zero period to allot for more electives. “I think this is super innovative, and I want to take all of these electives,” said board member Lindsay Thomasson. “I really appreciate the out-of-the-box thinking.” Board President Ruchi Medhekar called the changes “a solution to a problem that has existed for a long time.”

articles.text: Since I’ve come home for summer break after finishing my first year in university, I have often found myself pondering how different my life would be if I had chosen UC San Diego over St. Andrews in Scotland. Swapping weeks of endless grey skies and sheets of bone chilling rain for constant sunshine and miles of idyllic California coastline, I get swept up in this day dream. Especially when my 20-minute walk back to my dorm from the library is pitch dark despite it only being four o’clock in the afternoon, or when I saw my friends who chose schools in warmer climates posting on social media about the college experiences they had had thus far. This thought of ‘what if’ prompted me to think about the differences of my Scottish university experience to that of any other American college. When I think about the American college experience I think of my sister and my closest friend. My sister graduated from UC Santa Barbara and my good friend will be a junior at the University of Oregon. When my sister went to college, I was just starting high school and had no idea where I wanted to go to college. But listening to my sister tell stories about the daily sunset pilgrimages at UCSB where all the students would walk along Isla Vista’s coastline with their friends to unwind for the night. Or what it was like to live in a college town inhabited by students and all the interesting and sometimes crazy happenings that came with it. But what I understood from my sister’s stories was that college had the potential to be some of the freest and best years of young adulthood. With that information firmly rooted into my mind, I made up my mind to work toward what my dad called, the ‘Santa Barbara Experience.’ For most of high school, especially junior year, whenever I was asked where I wanted to go to college, I answered UCSB because I wanted to experience what my sister did, I wanted to feel that sense of a never-ending adventure. When I entered my senior year at Bentley School, my closest friend had started her first year at the University of Oregon. During our facetime calls when I was done complaining about the college application process, she would tell me about her college life. And like my sister, she had many exciting stories about college, like joining the Kappa Delta sorority and meeting some good friends because of it. She would tell me about the Oregon football games, about the different musical artists that came to perform on campus, and other first-year experiences. At the time I wanted nothing more than to have that kind of college journey. Both my sister’s and friend’s stories fueled me for the final push of college applications. On my list of colleges was one school that was an outlier among the rest, St. Andrews. In contrast to the other schools it was much smaller, only about 8,000 undergraduates, and was a more specialised research university. More importantly it was on the other side of the globe. From the first time my parents took me to London, I was enamoured. It had been my far, far-fetched dream since that trip to eventually go to school in the United Kingdom. It was the kind of goal that would be an intense up-hill battle. It wasn’t until my high school theater class made a trip to Edinburgh to the Fringe Festival my junior year, that I had found out about St. Andrews. Its application system had been altered to help accommodate international students, meaning that the only requirement I needed to fulfill was to supply an AP test score above a three. Nonetheless, it was hard to get into despite its accommodation. When I finally submitted my final application in December, I kept my expectations low on getting an offer from St. Andrews. To my surprise, two and a half months later I found myself at a crossroads. I had been offered acceptance at St. Andrews and UC San Diego (ironically UCSB, my sister’s school, rejected me). UC San Diego had been the type of school that I had been working towards – a big public state school in Southern California, while St. Andrews was a school I knew next to nothing about. Despite that, I took one of the biggest leaps of faith, dug my heels in, and chose to go to university on a different continent. Despite the attempts at reconsideration by my family, I stood by my choice; it was my childhood dream on the brink of coming true. Yet despite that I had a sense of anxiety; I had no idea what kind of school St. Andrews really was. I only knew that the town had three main streets, the furthest walk was 25 minutes, and that it was renowned for its School of International Relations. So as graduation from high school came and went, as I went through the steps of applying for a student visa, and coming to terms with the fact that I would be incredibly far from my family, I researched St. Andrews. In hindsight I should have done that before I applied, but there’s a reason the saying ‘there’s no time like the present’ exists. Come September, and I was about to start at a college where I really did not think I would end up, I spent the first few weeks recalling the stories my sister and friend had told me and eagerly awaited having those exact same experiences. But as the weeks stretched on, I found that they didn’t necessarily happen. I was getting disheartened, I had worked for four years to have the classic American college experience, only to find myself in a place where everything seemed different. My first semester in Scotland was spent adjusting to a new system of learning, grading, and teaching with occasional weekend excursions or pub nights with new found friends. All the while I would see my friends at American colleges out enjoying the things I thought I too should experience. As winter break rolled around I was at home again reunited with my family and friends. I first thought ‘what if?’ San Diego seemed like a dream to me then, I was wondering if I had made the wrong decision. I talked about it with my mother extensively, I sought the advice of my sister and my friend at Oregon. I even tried to think what my late grandmother would say to me. It was only after speaking with my sister for the umpteenth time that I was reminded that the college experience isn’t something handed to you tied up neatly with a prim bow on top, it was something you made. And as obvious as that sounds, I had lost sight of that concept. I had been so caught up in trying to make St. Andrews fit into a mold when it was in fact a star, and in that process I had overlooked everything that had made it different and special. So when I went back for spring semester, I went back with renewed vigour. articles.text: With the new school year approaching, the Class of 2027 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their athletic careers as a senior. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them when they return. EMMA CHAN Tennis Staff Photos Cole Carnazzo has been a huge part of the swimming team’s success over the last three years and enters his fourth year on the varsity team. COLE CARNAZZO Swimming Emma Chan enters her senior year after making school history, winning the school’s only WACC doubles title in the individual tournament alongside Samantha Huynh. With Chan, the Highlanders won the league’s regular season title with a 13-9 overall record while going 7-1 against league opponents. At the WACC Individual Tournament, Chan and Huynh beat Alameda’s Natalie Wong and Sophie Featherstone in the finals, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3. They also took down Naomi Lin and Caroline Sue of Alameda 6-4, 6-4 in the semifinals, won 7-6 (7-2), 6-3 over No. 4 seed Fiona Wood and Sloane Kau of Bishop O’Dowd in the quarterfinals, and opened the tournament with a heated 4-6, 6-2, 14-12 win over Berkeley’s Esra Abarbanel and Vera Ertel. Chan earned an honorable mention for All-League honors and was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in November. Cole Carnazzo is a big part of the boys’ swimming team’s renaissance over the last few years, helping the 200 medley team reach the CIF State Championship despite not competing in the meet. At the NCS Championship, Carnazzo helped the medley relay team place fourth of 16 finalists in 1:32.91 alongside Asher Takazawa, Nik Costello, and his younger brother, Connor Carnazzo. To reach the finals, the team placed third of 37 teams in 1:32.10. Cole Carnazzo also helped the Highlanders set a 200 medley relay league record at the Western Alameda County Conference Championship with a time of 1:31.81 in a field of 15 teams. He was also a part of PHS’ league title in the 400 freestyle relay, winning the event with a time of 3:09.02 against 16 other schools. He was the second leg of the event alongside Takazawa, Costello, and Dima Secor. CONNOR FREDERICKS Lacrosse Connor Fredericks will be a four-year starter on the boys’ lacrosse team come his senior season in the spring. He earned first-team All-League honors as a junior, and second-team honors as a sophomore and freshman. In 2026, Fredericks helped Piedmont go 7-8 overall and receive the No. 6 seed in the D2 NCS playoffs. They beat No. 11 Las Lomas 12-11 in a thrilling overtime win for the first round of the postseason, but lost 7-6 to No. 3 Miramonte in a heated quarterfinal. Fredericks scored five goals, two assists, and 10 ground balls in PHS’ win over Las Lomas, including winning the opening faceoff of overtime to set up the winning Golden Goal. He also logged three goals, had two assists, five ground balls, and won 12 face-offs their playoff loss to Miramonte. He was our honorable mention for Freshman of the Year in 2024. Emma Chan returns this fall as the defending WACC Doubles champion and a senior leader on the tennis team. Connor Fredericks enters his fourth year as a varsity starter on the lacrosse team, He was our 2024 honorable mention for Freshman of the Year.

Piedmont High’s football team is getting its summer training camp underway as they prepare for the approaching fall season. On Wednesday, June 24, Piedmont hosted San Lorenzo for a 7-on-7 scrimmage – scoring four touchdowns to SLZ’s three, while the junior varsity squad shutout the Grizzlies 2-0. The Highlanders are going through big changes in 2026. On top of losing nine seniors from last year’s team, they must replace quarterback Jimmy Lagios after he transferred to another school. “It’s my first time in five years that we won’t have a Lagios running the show,” said coach Jordan Seiden. “We’re a really young team and lost a lot of guys to graduation, but now’s the time for the young guys to step up. It’s been fun.” Taking all of the reps in Wednesday’s 7-on-7 was rising sophomore Cyrus Emanuelson at quarterback. Seiden mentioned that Emanuelson will be competing with Jonah Cha-Foster for the starting job, making this an important offseason. “Cyrus is in contention. Jonah is a super talented baseball player and also a talented quarterback; he’s a great fit for our system,” Seiden mentioned. “I just have to keep competing and working, I’ve been training with a coach. I’m not really worried about whether I get the [starting quarterback role, I just want to keep competing. I’m learning how to throw a tighter spiral and just how to bounce back from mistakes,” Emanuelson said. Emanuelson threw two touchdown passes to Diego Hurwitz, and one to Mateo Long and George Saunders. Hurwitz missed a portion of last season due to an injury, and he’s set to move up the Highlanders’ depth chart after the team lost its top two receivers from last season in Cash Panico and Jack Meyjes. “Last year, I was injured for half of the year and it required a lot of rebuilding. articles.text: Yaxel Lendeborg speaks excitedly about the prospect of joining the Warriors and teaming up with Steph Curry. At the 2026 NBA draft, the Warriors walked away winners, drafting Michigan forward Yaxel Lendeborg in the first round (No. 11) and Florida State forward Lajae Jones (No. 54) in the second round. The Warriors got an experienced win-now player in Lendeborg who will be featured in big moments throughout the upcoming season. Draft expert and writer for The Athletic, Sam Veccine, “loved” the Warriors’ selection of Lendeborg. He believes Lendeborg is one of the most talented defenders in the class. His passing ability will make head coach Steve Kerr’s life much easier. His age is not a worry for the Warriors, who are trying to compete next season as Steph continues to age. “I think we’re excited to add Yaxel to the program,” said Warriors General Manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. “I think I said it a week or so ago that we felt like being at 11 we’d get a really good player, and I think we did. He’s a guy that we feel fits with our system right away. Obviously being a more older, mature player, those types of guys you can expect to come in and have more of an impact than maybe some of the younger guys.” Lendeborg averaged 15.1 points — on a 64.6 true shooting percentage — as well as 6.8 rebounds and 3.2 assists in his junior year at Michigan. He’s expected to make an immediate impact on the team next year. Lendeborg had this to say about joining the Warriors. “It’s a full-circle moment for me. In 2016, I was a big Kyrie Irving guy, so I used to hate Steph Curry,” said Lendeborg. “Now that I’m actually going to be able to be on the same team with him, play and actually learn so much from him, it means a lot. “He’s a very great guy, a genuine person. It’s going to be an honor to be able to watch what he does in person.” Curry responded on Instagram to Lendeborg, stating, “Let’s go! Welcome to the Bay! I’m going to work hard to be your new favorite player,” adding a cry-laughing emoji to the end. Many experts believed Lendeborg was a top-five player in the draft class, but he fell due to being an older prospect at age 23. The Warriors got an objective steal at 11th overall, a player who could be one of the most impactful role players in the NBA. The Warriors’ second-round pick is not as well known as Lendeborg, but still has the potential to make an impact. This past season, Jones averaged 12.7 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. His 3-point shooting went from 3.7 attempts per game at St. Bonaventure to 5.1 percent for Florida State, but his percentage dropped to 32.5 percent. He’s a 6-foot-7 wing weighing 220 pounds. With injuries to Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody, there is a hole in the Warriors’ wing depth, and Jones could fill that. Currently, the Warriors’ only wings on the roster are Gui Santos and Yaxel Lendeborg. Jones could immediately be that 3rd or 4th wing on the roster that could fill in if there is an injury to anyone above him. Given GM Dunleavy’s track record with second-round picks, I’m very intrigued to see if Jones can make a significant impact down the line. Overall, as a Warriors fan, I am very satisfied with the draft decisions and excited to see how they fit in next season.

articles.text: Men’s soccer team to face Bosnia-Herzegovina today Photo courtesy of US Soccer The United States is looking strong going into its Round of 32 match against Bosnia and Herzegovina today. The 2026 World Cup’s Group Stage has now concluded and we’re charging through the first few days of the Round of 32. The knockout stage has had a thrilling start, with two of the top European sides falling in penalty kicks after Paraguay stunned Germany 4-3, and Morocco took down the Netherlands 3-2 after both matches ended regulation in a 1-1 draw. As of Post time, Mexico vs. Ecuador was the only Round of 32 match to not concluded in Tuesday’s slate of games. So, how did the Post do with its Group Stage predictions? We successfully guessed 27 teams to reach the Round of 32, 11 of 12 group winners, seven runner ups, and four of eight thirdplace teams. The tournament’s expansion to 48 teams certainly paid off for FIFA, with Cinderella teams like Cape Verde, South Africa, Paraguay, and DR Congo reaching the knockout stage. Here’s taking a look at my predictions for the upcoming Round of 32 and 16 matches, starting with the United States. No. 15 United States vs. No. 61 Bosnia and Herzegovina (Wednesday, 5 p.m.) The United States’ potential route to the quarterfinals, which would be their farthest journey since 2002, got a little bit harder after Belgium took the lead of its group over Egypt. Initially, I had the U.S. losing to Belgium in the Round of 16, but as of this point, I’m buying the States’ stock. Belgium has looked mighty shaky through the Group Stage, and I’m unconvinced about the European side. But, the U.S. must first get through Bosnia, which is coming off a 3-1 win over Qatar to close the Group Stage. I think the Stars and Stripes will get it done in Santa Clara on Wednesday night in a 3-1 win. No. 4 England vs. No. 41 DR Congo (Wednesday, 9 a.m.) The DRC has been quite the story in this year’s World Cup, proving FIFA right in expanding this year’s tournament size. They reached their first World Cup in 52 years, and qualified for the knockout stage for the first time ever by taking third in their group after tying Portugal 1-1 and beating Uzbekistan 3-1. But, I think the Cinderella story is over. England win, 4-nil. No. 10 Belgium vs. No. 18 Senegal (Wednesday, 1 p.m.) This might be the most difficult game to predict. Both squads have underperformed and didn’t look its best until their final group stage match against their weakest opponents, where Senegal beat Iraq 5-nil and Belgium won 5-1 over New Zealand. Senegal has had the tougher route in its group against France and Norway, so I’m going with the upset. Senegal wins 2-1. No. 3 Spain vs. No. 23 Austria (Thursday, 12 p.m.) I’m still standing on my guess for Spain to reach the semifinals despite not looking as illustrious as expected. Spain wins 2-0. Experts say the Warriors dominated this year’s NBA draft Yaxel Lendeborg speaks excitedly about the prospect of joining the Warriors and teaming up with Steph Curry. By Jake Lannon At the 2026 NBA draft, the Warriors walked away winners, drafting Michigan forward Yaxel Lendeborg in the first round (No. 11) and Florida State forward Lajae Jones (No. 54) in the second round. The Warriors got an experienced win-now player in Lendeborg who will be featured in big moments throughout the upcoming season. Draft expert and writer for The Athletic, Sam Veccine, “loved” the Warriors’ selection of Lendeborg. He believes Lendeborg is one of the most talented defenders in the class. His passing ability will make head coach Steve Kerr’s life much easier. His age is not a worry for the Warriors, who are trying to compete next season as Steph continues to age. “I think we’re excited to add Yaxel to the program,” said Warriors General Manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. “I think I said it a week or so ago that we felt like being at 11 we’d get a really good player, and I think we did. He’s a guy that we feel fits with our system right away. Obviously being a more older, mature player, those types of guys you can expect to come in and have more of an impact than maybe some of the younger guys.” Lendeborg averaged 15.1 points — on a 64.6 true shooting percentage — as well as 6.8 rebounds and 3.2 assists in his junior year at Michigan. He’s expected to make an immediate impact on the team next year. Lendeborg had this to say about joining the Warriors. “It’s a full-circle moment for me. In 2016, I was a big Kyrie Irving guy, so I used to hate Steph Curry,” said Lendeborg. “Now that I’m actually going to be able to be on the same team with him, play and actually learn so much from him, it means a lot. “He’s a very great guy, a genuine person. It’s going to be an honor to be able to watch what he does in person.” Curry responded on Instagram to Lendeborg, stating, “Let’s go! Welcome to the Bay! I’m going to work hard to be your new favorite player,” adding a cry-laughing emoji to the end. Many experts believed Lendeborg was a top-five player in the draft class, but he fell due to being an older prospect at age 23. The Warriors got an objective steal at 11th overall, a player who could be one of the most impactful role players in the NBA. The Warriors’ second-round pick is not as well known as Lendeborg, but still has the potential to make an impact. This past season, Jones averaged 12.7 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. His 3-point shooting went from 3.7 attempts per game at St. Bonaventure to 5.1 percent for Florida State, but his percentage dropped to 32.5 percent. He’s a 6-foot-7 wing weighing 220 pounds. With injuries to Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody, there is a hole in the Warriors’ wing depth, and Jones could fill that. Currently, the Warriors’ only wings on the roster are Gui Santos and Yaxel Lendeborg. Jones could immediately be that 3rd or 4th wing on the roster that could fill in if there is an injury to anyone above him. Given GM Dunleavy’s track record with second-round picks, I’m very intrigued to see if Jones can make a significant impact down the line. Overall, as a Warriors fan, I am very satisfied with the draft decisions and excited to see how they fit in next season.

articles.text: Young Musicians Chorus: Collegium Musicum (USA) The female choral group Young Musicians Chorus will perform in this year’s Golden Gate International Choral Festival. Founded in 2020, the group has developed a reputation for strong musicianship, challenging repertoire, musical character, and subtlety of interpretation. Young Musicians Chorus’s spotlight performance will take place July 16 at St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland. Young Musicians Chorus Collegium, the most-advanced of Young Musicians Chorus’s 5 levels, has been featured as artists in concerts with the San Francisco Choral Society, Viva la Musica, SF Choral Artists, and San Francisco Boys Chorus, and was the representative choir for last spring’s Foundation for Kodály Music Educators demonstration and concert. Founder and artistic director Betsy Marvit has created high standards for youth choral singing through her tenure of over 25 years at San Francisco Boys Chorus. At the Crowden Music Center in Berkeley, she ran a choral program for over 12 years and developed a passion for teaching choral music to young musicians. Young Musicians Chorus is a community choir with a shared goal of musical beauty, fun, and challenge, in an atmosphere of acceptance. They pay special attention musically to the social issues their students care about. It’s a small organization supported by the local community and fueled by the enthusiasm and artistry of its students. The group previously participated in the 2023 Golden Gate International Choral Festival, winning silver in the contemporary division. The Golden Gate International Choral Festival takes place locally from July 13 to July 18. Information on the concerts and spotlight choirs can be found on their website, including which concerts are free or have paid admission for the public. https://www.piedmontchoirs.org/ ggf-concerts-2026.

articles.text: Into the Woods premieres July 11. Berkeley Playhouse brings the classic Grimm fairytale Into the Woods to audiences next month. The musical tells the story of a baker and his wife who attempt to lift a family curse and have a child. They are visited by a witch who promises she can fulfill the request, but on her terms only. The couple must travel into the nearby woods and search for four items: a cow as white as milk, a cape as red as blood, hair as yellow as corn, and a slipper as pure as gold. The production features a cast of familiar fairytale characters, like Rapunzel, Cinderella, Jack, and Little Red Riding Hood. Photo by Thomas Campitelli Music and lyrics are by Stephen Sondheim for this play adaptation of James Lapine’s book of the same name. Cast includes actors in grades 7 through 12, including Azalea Campbell, Mia Wong, Ernst Wang, Kimiko Bearde-Xisin, Sofie Donati, Brenda Gonzalez, Chase Wilcox, Lourdes Verde Lombardo, Taylor Petri, Nevo Naftalin-Kelman, Sawyer Ciruli, Harper Taylor, Piper Lilquist, Elise Talbot, Keila Reeves, Ella Smithers, Jayden McAdams and Maeve Dey-Toth. articles.text: Immersive exhibition “Creating Home” on view now Kids enjoy free admission with the purchase of an adult ticket this summer at Filoli. For a limited time, children under age 14 can visit Filoli’s historic estate and garden and view the nonprofit organization’s newest property-wide exhibition, “Creating Home,” which explores themes of home, habitat and belonging. “Creating Home,” on view throughout the summer, spans the historic estate’s gardens, house, redwood groves and natural campus, featuring interactive installations, storytelling experiences and educational programming designed to encourage visitors to engage with the people, animals and trees that shape the property. The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by California artist Jayson Fann. Constructed from naturally found wood and organic materials, the sculptural works are inspired by bird nests, tree hollows and other natural shelters found throughout the landscape. “This summer at Filoli is all about exploration, discovery, and inspiration,” Kara Newport, president and CEO of Filoli, said in a press release. “With ‘Creating Home,’ guests will uncover interactive installations inspired by the animals, trees, and stories that shape Filoli’s landscape, while ‘Kids Go Free’ makes it even easier for families to spend The centerpiece of the exhibition is a large-scale outdoor installation by artist Jayson Fann. the day outside together. From the gardens and historic house to the redwoods and trails, there’s something around every corner waiting to spark curiosity and joy.” The exhibition opens alongside Filoli’s Kids Go Free summer promotion, aimed at encouraging family visits throughout the season. Tickets must be reserved in advance online, and the offer is valid for daytime admission only. In addition to Fann’s outdoor installations, visitors will find immersive room displays inside the historic house highlighting the stories of staff members who helped shape Filoli. Other interactive elements include projected ballroom dance lessons, listening stations featuring imagined historic conversations and opportunities for guests to share family stories. Storytelling signage, daily staff talks and family-focused educational activities will also highlight local wildlife, notable trees and the ecosystems found across the estate. “I have worked with naturally found wood since early childhood, growing up along the Platte River,” Fann said. “This lifelong practice of listening deeply to the land, shaped by flowing water, wind, lightning, thunder, and the rhythms of the landscape, continues to inform my approach to nest building. In Creating Home, these elements come together to remind us that building, belonging, and care all arise through relationships with the world around us.” For more information, visit https://filoli.org/.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is celebrating Agave in July, with speaker events, webinars, tours and workshops celebrating the iconic genus all throughout the month. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants, including Agave. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The garden is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Agave Fest celebrates one of Ruth’s most prized plants, native to the arid regions of North, South and Central Americas. See a list of daily events below. July 11 - Curator-led lector Ruth Bancroft Garden Curator Brian Kemble will share his insights on agaves as powerful focal point plants, the wide range of genera found in the nursery trade and the fascinating stories behind rare and unusual species. Kemble has worked with the gardens for 45 years and oversees Brian Kemble thousands of agave and succulent species that grow in the garden’s three acres. Following the talk, a limited-capacity tour will offer an up-close look at select specimens, along with a special sale featuring rare agaves from Kemble’s private greenhouse. The lecture begins at 10 a.m. July 11 - Pop-up plant sale A curated selection of unique agaves from the private greenhouse collections of Ruth Bancroft Curator Brian Kemble and Garden Manager Walker Young will be available for purchase between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. July 18 - Mezcal tasting Join garden staff and agave experts for an evening guided tour focused on the “spirit” of agave. Produced primarily in Oaxaca and eight other regulated Mexican states, Mezcal is commonly made from the Espadín agave, but wild varieties like Tobalá and Tepeztate are also used. Kemble and Susan Coss, co-founder of Mezcalistas, lead the tour which precedes an assorted Mezcal tasting. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/agave-fest/ to learn more about Agave Fest.
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft celebrates month-long Agave Fest in July

articles.text: Music at Kohl Mansion announced its 44th anniversary season, featuring eight performances by internationally acclaimed chamber music ensembles and artists from October 18, 2026 through May 2, 2027. The Burlingame concert series will present Sunday evening performances at 7 p.m., showcasing returning ensembles alongside debut appearances by several artists. Performances are held in the historic Kohl Mansion, also known as The Oaks, which was built in 1914 and is located at 2750 Adeline Drive in Burlingame. The mansion was listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its architecture and social and cultural significance to the local area in 1982, and provides a unique and intimate setting for chamber music concerts. “Our 44th season honors the rich traditions of chamber music while looking ahead to an exciting and dynamic future,” Music at Kohl Mansion Executive Director Patricia Kristof Moy said in a press release. “We are thrilled to welcome remarkable artists from across the United States and Europe and to invite audiences into the uniquely personal experience that chamber music offers.” Among the season highlights are the Music at Kohl Mansion debuts of the Neave Trio on November 15 and the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet on January 17, 2027. The Neave Trio will perform a program featuring works by early 20th-century Croatian composer Dora Pejačević, while the Thunder Egg Consort Piano Quartet will present the local premiere of Hard Winter/ Holler and Stomp by violist and composer Kenji Bunch. When President Kennedy made a speech in the German city of Berlin, he said “today I am a Berliner.” The immediate reaction of some of The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet the people was a subdued laugh. Then they cheered. The reason that they laughed was because he actually said “today I am a jelly donut.” “A Berliner” is a jelly donut. What he should’ve said is: Ich bin Berliner. The Germans leave out the article “ein”. Other foods seem to imply personal characteristics. Two of them are “jerk“ and “haggis.”. Close on their heels are the violence of “poke and punch.” Animals might enter the picture when you are in Wales and you order Welsh rarebit (pronounced “rabbit”). This delicious cheese dish was a specialty of my mother. Some foods sound scatological. The eastern European Jewish dumpling known as Kreplach is notable. I was in a French restaurant and the Maître D pronounced crepe as “crap.” This is a Persian eggplant dish and he wasn’t Kuku. Other excellent foods have suggestive names. “Bulgur”, cock-aleekie, and matzah balls suggest other things. A woman who has served matzah balls wondered how large the animal was. Can you imagine how a mafioso would order mofongo. It sounds like an Italian insult. In reality it is a Puerto Rican type of plantain. Open the vindaloo for some fresh air. Your adventure is about to begin. What? You have objections? Well… If you don’t like it, you can “lumpia.” All of the above are “njoki” and that’s no joke, especially when you are in Yugoslavia. So enjoy your plate of dumplings. To paraphrase the advice of a noted travel expert… keep eating. articles.text: Movies about journalism often miss their mark. But The Post gets it just right, placing it in the same realm as what was a superb film about the Boston Diocese pedophilia scandal titled Spotlight. And there was, of course, a film that will be forever memorable, the iconic All the President’s Men. But what makes The Post so significant is, ultimately, not the story or the actors (Tom Hanks and Meryl Streep are excellent as Ben Bradlee, editor, and Katherine Graham, owner of the paper) but the timeless context. In other words, though it takes place in 1971, the importance of a free press today is as relevant as it was then. Perhaps more so. The press, also known as the Fourth Estate, is as essential to a vital and robust democracy as are the other three branches of government. In 1971, Richard Nixon loathed the press, especially the Post and the NY Times. As one character says emphatically (Bruce Greenwood as Robert McNamara), if you print the story you are now in possession of, Nixon will use all of the power of his presidency to destroy your paper. He spoke those words to Katherine Graham who understood that the decision facing her – whether to publish what became known as The Pentagon Papers, and, in the aggregate, demonstrated that the government had been lying about Vietnam for decades. Printing the story would clearly place the paper in harm’s way, a paper that had been in her family since the 1930s. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and MXKA performs at OMCA next week. Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. San Leandro-based artist MXKA performs on July 10, delivering regional Mexican rhythms and R&B vocals. A Cumbia Wepa dance lesson led by Mireille Ruiz takes place throughout the evening. Visitors can also participate in an art-making activation led by artist Jason Powell-Smith, browse and purchase original artworks and special-edition pieces, meet other artists and staff, and learn more about NIAD Art Center’s work supporting professional artists with disabilities. articles.text: Nuclear Physicist, Navy Captain, Lawyer, and Academic George Malcolm Moore was a nuclear physicist, a Navy Captain, a lawyer, and an academic. His unique combination of knowledge and experience allowed him to reach and impact people across the globe. He passed away peacefully on June 23rd, 2026, after a multiple-year battle with cancer with his family at his side at his home in Piedmont, CA. George was born in Berkeley, CA at Alta Bates Hospital, the same hospital where his mother and later his children were born. He grew up in a Navy family, living primarily in Oakland, Monterey, and Coronado and attending 13 different schools before graduating high school. As a young man he distinguished himself as both a scholar and an athlete. After graduating Coronado High School in 1962, he entered the U.S. Naval Academy where he finished first academically in the class of 1966, earning prizes for mathematics, chemistry, physics, and history. As an athlete he excelled at football, rowing, track and field, and golf. George had a lifelong enthusiasm for aviation and dreamed of being a fighter pilot before vision deterioration forced a change in his trajectory. George was a Fulbright Scholar at the University of Amsterdam, obtained a PhD in nuclear engineering from UC Berkeley, and served on active duty in Vietnam before transitioning to the Navy Reserve and working for the Department of Energy at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. In his lab career he focused on weapons design and countering nuclear and terrorism threats, taking particular joy in his work with the Nuclear Emergency Support Team. As a Captain in the Naval Reserve George led a Mobile Inshore Undersea Warfare Unit, a Commissioned Naval Unit, and a Fleet Training Group Detachment. George left the lab to obtain his law degree from UC Berkeley and pursued a career as a defense attorney in both energy and aviation litigation, practicing as an in-house counsel for the Pacific Gas and Electric Company and later as a partner at the aviation litigation firm Kenny and Markowitz in San Francisco. It was during this period he and his wife, Stella Kennedy, raised their children Greg and Sarah Moore in Piedmont, CA. Following 9/11 George returned to Livermore Lab and then transitioned to the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna, Austria, focusing his diplomatic work on nuclear nonproliferation and security. He later became a Scientist in Residence at the Middlebury Institute for International Studies in Monterey, CA where he taught and published on nuclear nonproliferation, security, and drone technology. His work during this period gave him the opportunity to travel the world with Stella which they enjoyed immensely. His contributions will continue through his students who now work in government agencies, the United Nations, universities, think tanks, military and law enforcement units, and nonprofits worldwide. As a father George was a devoted coach, scouting volunteer, and unfailing attendee of Greg and Sarah’s many sporting, scouting, and performing arts events. He was enduringly supportive of Greg and Sarah’s many pursuits and provided constant encouragement for their growth and exploration. He was noted by his family for possessing a remarkable ability to connect with animals and small children. George loved dogs and had a special affection for the Boxer breed, which he raised, bred, and showed. He was an avid amateur pilot and a licensed nuclear reactor engineer. George is survived by his wife of 46 years, Stella Kennedy, of Piedmont, CA, his son Greg Moore of Davis, CA, his daughter Sarah Moore of Falls Church, VA, and his Boxer Hattie. He will be laid to rest in Arlington National Cemetery. In lieu of a service, those wishing to share any memories or reflections on George for the family are encouraged to send any thoughts, photos, or recordings to george.m.moore.memorial@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Janet Mendenhall died at her home in Walnut Creek on April 9, 2026. She was 105. Born on December 15, 1920 in Carbondale, Pennsylvania, she was the daughter of Orville and Elsie Ackerly. Her siblings were Helen, William, and Francis. During her elementary school years, the family moved to Piedmont, California, where Janet attended Wildwood Elementary School, Piedmont High School and ultimately graduated from the University of California in Berkeley with a degree in geography. After graduation, she joined the Marine Corps and was stationed at the weather station in Cherry Point, North Carolina working for the OSS. Upon return to Piedmont, she met Charles I. Mendenhall through the Piedmont Community Church choir. They married in 1951 and had two children, Bryce and Jan. Janet is survived by her daughter, Jan Moestue and her grandchildren Benjamin and Amylia. She was also blessed with three step great grandchilJanet Alice Mendenhall dren Brayden, Aiden and Ellie. She is predeceased by her husband, Charles and her son Bryce. Janet lived in Rossmoor for the last 23 years and was a strong supporter of the Diablo Valley Symphony. A memorial service will be held on Saturday, July 18 at 1 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church. Janet was a member of the church from age 16 to 105 years old. A life of love and strength, she was an inspiration to all who knew her.

articles.text: Tamra C. Hege, age 87, died peacefully at St. Paul’s Tower after a lengthy battle with congestive heart failure. She was born in Concord, CA June 18, 1938, to Florence Gertrude Kennerly Cummings and William Louis Cummings. Tamra graduated in 1960 from UC Berkeley with a zoology degree and later received a master’s degree in liberal studies from Mills College in 1997. She taught high school science at Hamlin’s School in San Francisco from 1962-1967. She moved to Piedmont in 1972 and was a lifelong volunteer for numerous organizations including Piedmont School Board (1982-1990), Piedmont Planning Commission (2001- 2007), Member of the Oakla nd Mu seu m’s Women’s Board (1999-present, President 2007-2009), Piedmont League of Women Voters (President 1980-1981, 1992-1994, 2010- 2012), and active member of Lake Merritt United Methodist Church. She was married to Dr. John Steele Hege for 56 years. They enjoyed a lifetime of backpacking, sailing, and raising three children. Tamra is survived by her daughters Laura Goodale (Michael) and Anne Hege (Grant Tompkins), and her five grandchildren Matt Goodale, Chris Goodale (Sydney), Dorothea Tompkins, Vera Tompkins, and Johnnie Tompkins. She was predeceased by her husband John Steele Hege in 2017 and her son John Raymond Hege of the Oakland Police Department who was killed in the line of duty in 2009. Tamra is also survived by two sisters Lana Laessig and Erin Wells (Larry), as well as her brother Ross Cummings (Andrea) and two nephews. A memorial service will be held on Saturday, July 11th, 2026, at 3 pm at the Lake Merritt United Methodist Church, 1255 First Ave, Oakland, CA 94606. In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Friends of the Oakland Public Library or the Oakland Museum of California.

articles.text: In the heart of Napa Valley’s Calistoga region, Davis Estates represents the blending of Napa’s historic past with a modern vision for the future. Built on a century-old vineyard property along the Silverado Trail, the family-owned winery has transformed a historic site into one of Napa Valley’s newest destinations for fine wine, hospitality, and estategrown Cabernet Sauvignon. The story of Davis Estates begins with Mike Davis, whose lifelong connection to Napa Valley inspired a dream of creating a world-class family winery. In 2011, Davis and his family purchased the historic estate and began an ambitious restoration project, revitalizing the property while preserving its character and agricultural heritage. The winery officially opened as Davis Estates in 2014. Today, the 155-acre Calistoga estate showcases the dramatic diversity of Napa Valley’s northern landscape. Rising from the valley floor to elevations of more than 1,100 feet, the property includes volcanic soils, varied microclimates, and hillside terrain that provide ideal conditions for growing premium Bordeaux varieties, especially Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and Merlot. Davis Estates has earned attention for its commitment to producing elegant, age-worthy wines with a strong sense of place. The winery has worked with acclaimed winemaking talent, including Philippe Melka, whose Bordeau x-i nspi red approach emphasizes vineyard expression and careful craftsmanship. Beyond the wines, Davis Estates offers visitors an experience that celebrates Napa Valley’s history and hospitality. Guests can enjoy tastings overlooking the vineyards, explore the restored historic barn, visit the caves, and experience food-andwine pairings designed to highlight the estate’s wines. While many Napa wineries trace their roots back generations, Davis Estates represents a different kind of legacy: a family’s determination to restore a historic property and create something lasting. With its combination of heritage, sustainability, and world-class Cabernet, Davis Estates has quickly become a distinctive voice in the continuing story of Napa Valley wine. articles.text: Alaska Mission Trip exceeds expectations What happens when you send a group of students more than 2,000 miles from home to serve others, experience a new culture, and grow in their faith? From June 5–12, a team of students and leaders from Piedmont Community Church set out to answer that question in Fairbanks, Alaska, as part of a pilot mission trip that may help shape the future of student missions at our church. Designed as a “beta test” for a potential new annual high school mission experience, the trip provided students with opportunities to serve the local community, learn about Alaska’s unique history and cultures, build lasting friendships, and discover how God can work through ordinary acts of service in extraordinary ways. For many years our Mexico Mission Trip was a cornerstone experience for students. However, increasing logistical challenges and changing policies among key partners led us to begin exploring new opportunities that would continue to provide meaningful service, faith formation, and cultural engagement. This year, a small group of students familiar with our church and community were invited to participate and provide candid feedback on whether Alaska could become the future home of our annual high school mission trip. Meri Schreiber splits firewood for a Fairbanks resident during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. Under the guidance of Next Step Ministries staff member Ava, students helped prepare and stack wood to help local residents stay warm through the Alaskan winter. Another important consideration was accessibility. One of our goals in evaluating future mission opportunities is ensurIncoming seniors Evie Hicks, Cora Brozowski-Schrader, and Clara Shum share a smile during Piedmont Community Church’s Alaska Mission Trip. ing that as many students as possible can participate. The Alaska trip was offered at a significantly lower price point than many traditional mission experiences, helping reduce financial barriers while still providing a meaningful week of service, spiritual growth, cultural learning, and community impact. As we look toward the future, creating opportunities that are both transformational and accessible remains a priority. Partnering with Next Step Ministries, a national organization that creates Christ-centered service experiences for students, our team spent three days working alongside residents and community organizations throughout Fairbanks. Students served at the Fairbanks Rescue Mission, where they power washed buildings, planted flowers, raked grounds, and sorted donations. They also worked directly with local residents, cutting, splitting, and stacking firewood, clearing brush, and helping prepare properties for the long Alaskan winter. One of the most memorable projects involved splitting and stacking approximately three cords of firewood at each of two homes. Both residents shared that the wood would help carry them through the harsh Alaskan winter—a powerful reminder that simple acts of service can have a lasting impact. One of the most meaningful aspects of the week was the opportunity to work alongside the people of Fairbanks rather than simply for them. Through conversations, shared meals, and service projects, students gained a deeper understanding of the community and the challenges many residents face. For Clara Shum, a soon-to-be senior who also participated in Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico Mission Trip, the experience highlighted the connection between service and community impact.

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends, and then chatting about it when the lights come up. The Flix Fest meets on the second Thursday of each month, and offers movies in a comfortable setting, with lively discussion afterwards. This July’s selection is American Graffiti, a coming-of-age portrayal of the 1962 teen hot-rod cruising culture. Director George Lucas wrote the film based on his experience during his high school years in Modesto. To develop a film from this period Lucas received encouragement from Francis Coppola to both direct and write the screenplay. Coppola agreed to produce the film and satisfy the financial concerns Universal Studios had for Lucas, then an unknown filmmaker. Written in just 3 weeks and filmed mostly in Petaluma, the film was nominated for 5 Oscars and grossed $61 million with a $750,000 budget. The movie uses little-known actors who later became major stars. The screenplay works well because it cleverly pairs up characters who are opposites. Terry the Toad (Charles Martin Smith), the lovable but clumsy nerd, spends the evening with Debby (Candy Clark), the “fast” girl, who isn’t exactly the sharpest tool in the shed. Meanwhile, John Milner (Paul Le Mat), tough guy, hot-rod cruiser, babysits Carol (Mackenzie Phillips), the funny, precocious, pre-teen. Then there’s Curt (Richard Dreyfuss), a cleancut kid and budding intellectual on his way to college, searching for the hot blond in a Thunderbird, but instead gets adopted by a group of hoodlums from the Pharaohs gang. Finally, Laurie and Steve (Cindy Williams and Ron Howard), the Homecoming Queen and popular jock are in crisis mode regarding their high school romance. Steve is looking to spread his wings in college the coming year. The conflict almost turns into a disaster when Laurie gets into a hot rod driven by the reckless street racer Bob Falfa (Harrison Ford). Who was the personality that unified all the scenes and stories? Lucas recruited legendary late-night disk jockey Wolfman Jack, played by himself, as the beloved radio voice among teens nationwide. His mysterious voice throughout the soundtrack guided them as they cruised through the night, creating a sense of closeness as he called out dedications, introduced new sounds, and spun away rock-and-roll tunes. American Graffiti stands out because it used the 1960s Top 40 rock and roll hits to tell the story. song, the soundtrack truly brings the spirit of the 60s to life. The film ends with an epilogue scroll that answers the question we all ask ourselves at our class reunions, “Whatever happened to….?” Common to each character listed are the role reversals they experienced after graduating from high school, matching Lucas’s own switch from auto mechanic to filmmaker. American Graffiti will be screened on Thursday, July 9, at 1 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Ave. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m., and the movie is free for anyone over age 18. This year’s event, starting at 11:00 a.m, marks its 59th year of fun and celebration with the theme “Independence Day the Piedmont Way”. In 1965, Dick Johnson, chairman of the Recreation Commission, began the parade after noticing a lull in patriotism during the Vietnam War years. From the beginning, the parade included marching bands, our favorite being the bagpipe bands, antique cars, and neighborhood participation, sometimes with elaborate floats. The parade ends at Piedmont Park, with celebratory speeches, lively music, tasty food stands, and plenty of space to enjoy a holiday picnic with friends & family. Come out and enjoy the festivities! MORTGAGE MONEY… Our “go-to” Mortgage Money Broker, BRADY THOMAS, LA SALLE MORTGAGE, has this to share this month: If your home has an ADU, a pool, or a view, you’ve probably wondered what it’s actually worth. The honest answer is: it depends on what buyers in your neighborhood have proven they’ll pay for it. That’s how appraisers figure it out. They pull sales of similar homes without the feature, then pull sales of similar homes with it. The difference between those two numbers is what your feature is actually contributing to your value. Not what it cost to build. Not what you think it’s worth. What the market has shown it will pay. A pool in one zip code might add $40,000. In another, almost nothing. A view can swing value by 10%… or barely move the needle. If you’re thinking about selling, this is the question worth asking before you price it.

articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike team will be riding in this year’s 4th of July Parade. Their first year in the parade was in 2023. The nonprofit organization’s focus is to get kids to have fun riding bikes. The group provides an opportunity weekly for high school and middle school students to learn to mountain bike. The umbrella organization for the team is called the National Interscholastic Cycling Association (NICA). NICA is a nationwide organization that started in Berkeley, CA, in 2009. The Piedmont Mountain Bike team is in the Central Conference of the Norcal league within NICA. The organization hosts two teams: a high school team and a development team consisting of kids in middle school or younger. Currently, the teams have 20 members each. The high school team’s season is four races from December to May with a championship race to end the year. This past season, the team finished 6th in their division at the 2026 NorZachary Carter, team co-captain in the upcoming season, racing at Exchequer near La Grange, CA. A picture of the team after participation in the 2025 4th of July parade. Development Coach Ode Bernstein and a parent hoist the wooden bike ramp that riders use for jumps during their parade appearance. cal High School Championships and 2nd overall. “It was just super awesome to see all the kids get really strong,” said Vanessa Oklejas, a representative of the Piedmont Mountain Bike team. “As the season goes on, they get in better and better condition, and they get faster and faster. So I remember towards the end of the season, the coaches were really sweating. They’re like ‘My gosh, they’re killing me.’ They’re just getting super fast.” Now that the season is over, the team focuses its attention on its participation in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade. The teams ride their bikes down Highland Avenue, doing tricks like a wheelie to excite the crowd. They usually bring a ramp to do jumps off of or a limbo stick to see how low they can go on their bikes. The team plans to hand out promotional material to highlight the team. “The crowd seems to like it. I think the middle school kids get the most enjoyment out of it. Getting them to do jumps and wheelies and the limbo is nothing. I think the bigger thing is getting them to the start line,” said Oklejas. Oklejas shared a memory of last year’s parade highlighting the importance of including everyone who wants to ride a bike. “What I really loved about last year was that there was a father who got in touch because his son wasn’t quite old enough to ride with the development team, but really wanted to be on that parade, and he had the best freaking time. He just loved it. He’s a fifth grader riding with big kids going off the ramp on, I mean, he just had a wonderful time,” she said. The mountain bike team encourages anyone interested to come and try it out. They host adventure rides before the season on Saturdays or Sundays. They offer loaner bikes to anyone who doesn’t have a bike. “It’s open to everybody. It’s really just come out and try it out,” said Oklejas. More information on the team can be found on their website: https://www.piedmontmtb.com/. Riders Mina Herrgott and Olivia Bailey on the race course at Six Sigma Ranch and Winery. articles.text: adjusting to being far from home again, but after the adjustment period. I found that everything about St. Andrews that I had been trying to change was what made it amazing. The sunset pilgrimages became walks along Lade Braes, a nature walk along a creek, Greek life became societies (fancy name for clubs) and sports teams, and formal events became society balls with ceilidh dancing. I soon began to experience the feeling of adventure and belonging I had been chasing. University was becoming something I looked forward to experiencing instead of dreading its contrasts to what my friends back home in the States had. While there are many aspects of upper education that differ between the US and the UK, what stays consistent is how much fun and growth you can have when you embrace the experience instead of fighting it. More importantly, the thought of ‘what if’ became a lighthearted gameplay scenario rather than the taunting threat it once was. I still think about San Diego, but now it’s a passing thought. As the fall term creeps closer to my second year at University, I find myself excited more than anything. Despite being in a place the opposite of where I thought I would end up, I find myself forging the experiences I have always wanted. Larissa Edel is a Piedmont resident and a former Piedmont Post intern.
